title: Beak Buffet: Parent Guide
endLine: Different beak shapes work well for different foods.

scenes.tts: How well can a clothespin pick up floating cereal? Give your child a chance to try it. Then see what happens when you offer a slotted spoon.
scenes.caption: How well can a clothespin pick up floating cereal? Give your child a chance to try it. Then see what happens when you offer a slotted spoon.
scenes.visual: Open on a schematic overhead view of a clothespin above a bowl of floating cereal loops. Let the loops drift as the clothespin lowers. A slotted spoon slides in alongside it.
scenes.narration: How well can a clothespin pick up floating cereal? Give your child a chance to try it. Then see what happens when you offer a slotted spoon.

scenes.visual: Camera pulls smoothly back over the same kitchen table. High-contrast bold title 'Beak Buffet' appears in the upper center while five clean tool silhouettes (clothespin, slotted spoon, straw, tongs, tweezers) settle gently along the bottom edge, then the title fades as the table stays in place.

scenes.tts: In about thirty-five minutes at the table, your child tests five kitchen tools as bird beaks. They practice guessing first, counting fairly, and comparing results. They also connect simple kitchen models to real birds outside.
scenes.caption: In about thirty-five minutes at the table, your child tests five kitchen tools as bird beaks. They practice guessing first, counting fairly, and comparing results. They also connect simple kitchen models to real birds outside.
scenes.visual: Same overhead kitchen table. A friendly schematic clock dial sweeps gently to thirty-five minutes in the top corner. Three crisp icon badges transform in sequence beside the table tools: a thought bubble ('Guess first'), tally marks ('Count fairly'), and a schematic bird silhouette matching a kitchen tool ('Match real birds'). Keep at most five elements on screen with slow ambient motion.
scenes.narration: In about thirty-five minutes at the table, your child tests five kitchen tools as bird beaks. They practice guessing first, counting fairly, and comparing results. They also connect simple kitchen models to real birds outside.

scenes.tts: Stay with your child throughout. Keep small pieces and water containers away from children under four. Small pieces can choke them. Call nine one one if choking. Check food allergies before setup. Skip red kidney beans. Keep all station items out of mouths.
scenes.caption: Stay with your child throughout. Keep small pieces and water containers away from children under four. Small pieces can choke them. Call nine one one if choking. Check food allergies before setup. Skip red kidney beans. Keep all station items out of mouths.
scenes.visual: Show the small pieces and water containers set back on the kitchen table. Add a compact choking safety card with the emergency number before showing setup.

scenes.tts: Set five stations around the table. Put dry lima or pinto beans in a shallow dish. Float cereal loops in a bowl of water. Put pasta fish in a pan with three centimeters of water. Cut any sponge yourself. Press yarn halfway into play dough.
scenes.caption: Set five stations around the table. Put dry lima or pinto beans in a shallow dish. Float cereal loops in a bowl of water. Put pasta fish in a pan with three centimeters of water. Cut any sponge yourself. Press yarn halfway into play dough.
scenes.visual: On the table, pan across a shallow bean dish, a bowl of floating cereal and a baking pan of shallow water with pasta fish. Show an adult hand cutting the optional sponge, then show play dough with yarn and a narrow plastic bottle of water.
scenes.narration: Set five stations around the table. Put dry lima or pinto beans in a shallow dish. Float cereal loops in a bowl of water. Put pasta fish in a pan with three centimeters of water. Cut any sponge yourself. Press yarn halfway into play dough.

scenes.tts: Set out a clothespin, slotted spoon, straw, tongs, and tweezers. Every child needs their own straw. Fill a narrow plastic bottle with water. Set an empty cup beside it.
scenes.caption: Set out a clothespin, slotted spoon, straw, tongs, and tweezers. Every child needs their own straw. Fill a narrow plastic bottle with water. Set an empty cup beside it.
scenes.visual: Line up the five tools on the same table. Show the narrow plastic bottle, a straw and the empty nectar cup beside it.
scenes.narration: Set out a clothespin, slotted spoon, straw, tongs, and tweezers. Every child needs their own straw. Fill a narrow plastic bottle with water. Set an empty cup beside it.

scenes.tts: Give your child a small cup to hold in one hand and a tool to hold in the other. Move food to the cup using only the tool. In this game the cup is the bird’s stomach.
scenes.caption: Give your child a small cup to hold in one hand and a tool to hold in the other. Move food to the cup using only the tool. In this game the cup is the bird’s stomach.
scenes.visual: Use a schematic close-up of two hands. Show one hand holding the cup and the other lifting a bean into it with the clothespin.
scenes.narration: Give your child a small cup to hold in one hand and a tool to hold in the other. Move food to the cup using only the tool. In this game the cup is the bird’s stomach.

scenes.tts: Start with pond food. Look at the clothespin and the slotted spoon. Which do you think will pick up more floating cereal in the same time?
scenes.caption: Start with pond food. Look at the clothespin and the slotted spoon. Which do you think will pick up more floating cereal in the same time?
scenes.visual: Frame the bowl from above, with a clothespin and a slotted spoon to either side. Show the question “Which picks up more?” and leave the cereal drifting.
scenes.narration: Start with pond food. Look at the clothespin and the slotted spoon. Which do you think will pick up more floating cereal in the same time?

scenes.visual: Hold the table view with both tools and the question. Let the cereal drift for the full pause.

scenes.tts: At each station, have your child pick three tools. Ask, “Which beak do you think will get the most food?” Write down their guess. Try each tool for thirty seconds. Count what lands in the cup, then tip it back.
scenes.caption: At each station, have your child pick three tools. Ask, “Which beak do you think will get the most food?” Write down their guess. Try each tool for thirty seconds. Count what lands in the cup, then tip it back.
scenes.visual: Start at the pond bowl with the tools from the question and a third tool. Show a written guess, tools moving pieces into the cup, a schematic timer and pieces tipped back after the tally.
scenes.narration: At each station, have your child pick three tools. Ask, “Which beak do you think will get the most food?” Write down their guess. Try each tool for thirty seconds. Count what lands in the cup, then tip it back.

scenes.tts: Dip the straw in the bottle and cover the top with a finger. Lift it over the empty cup and uncover it. Count each strawful. The straw models a hummingbird’s reach. A hummingbird uses its tongue to collect nectar.
scenes.caption: Dip the straw in the bottle and cover the top with a finger. Lift it over the empty cup and uncover it. Count each strawful. The straw models a hummingbird’s reach. A hummingbird uses its tongue to collect nectar.
scenes.visual: Move to the narrow bottle and empty cup. Follow a hand dipping, covering, lifting and releasing the straw. Add a tally when the water lands. Bring in a schematic hummingbird with its tongue reaching into a flower.

scenes.tts: Check the pond counts first. Circle the best tool for each food. Different beak shapes work well for different foods. A cardinal cracks seeds. A mallard strains food from water. A heron grabs fish. A hummingbird reaches nectar. A wren picks insects off bark.
scenes.caption: Check the pond counts first. Circle the best tool for each food. Different beak shapes work well for different foods. A cardinal cracks seeds. A mallard strains food from water. A heron grabs fish. A hummingbird reaches nectar. A wren picks insects off bark.
scenes.visual: Return to the clothespin and slotted spoon. Show the recorded counts side by side and circle the tool with the higher count. Then pair each kitchen tool with the corresponding bird and food. Show a northern cardinal, mallard, great blue heron, ruby-throated hummingbird and Carolina wren.

scenes.tts: If your child asks about changing beaks, try this. “Can you grow longer fingers to reach a high shelf?” A bird’s bill can grow and wear down during its life. A change in food cannot make one bird grow a different kind of bill. Over many generations, bill shapes can change across a group.

scenes.tts: Keep straws out of mouths and tweezer tips down and away from faces. Skip toothpicks and other sharp points. Wipe up spills and pick up dropped pieces right away. Empty the bowls and pan when you finish. Wash hands with soap and water.

scenes.visual: Return to the table. Show a straw releasing water, tweezers pointed down, and an adult wiping up a spill. Show the adult emptying the bowl and pan and end with hands being washed with soap.

scenes.tts: Ask, “What helped one tool work better?” Your child can use the counts to explain what they noticed. Watch how the tools move, too. A heron waits for a fish to come close.
